results.corrected_extracted: 123 studies were included (one a prospective cohort study, the rest RCTs; 22 803 participants); naltrexone was studied in 53 (n = 9140), with 44 placebo-controlled trials. Across all 123 studies (the article gives no figures for the naltrexone trials alone), treatment lasted 12 to 52 weeks and mean age was usually in the 40s; participants met criteria for alcohol dependence in the vast majority of trials and were mostly enrolled after detoxification or at least 3 days of abstinence. Most studies included psychosocial co-interventions, so effect sizes reflect the added benefit of medication beyond psychosocial interventions and placebo.
results.note: Scope fix, no number changed: the 12–52-week range and the other characteristics describe all 123 studies. The pooled oral-naltrexone trials lasted 12–24 weeks (Figures 2–3, pp. 1893–1894), so this anchor cannot support the claim's '12 to 52 weeks'.

results.corrected_extracted: Most participants met DSM-III or DSM-IV criteria for alcohol dependence, likely moderate to severe disorder in DSM-5 terms, so applicability to mild disorder is uncertain; mean age was generally in the 40s and there was no evidence on whether benefit differs by age or other characteristics. Of 44 placebo-controlled naltrexone trials, 27 were in the US and 8 in Europe. Few studies were rated at low risk of bias (8 of 123; 4 of 53 naltrexone studies); most were medium risk because of incomplete reporting of sequence generation, allocation concealment, fidelity, adherence or outcome-assessor masking.
